title: Joining Multiple Tables 🧩
description: Chain JOINs to query from three or more tables in a single statement.

slides.title: Beyond Two Tables 🌉
slides.content:
# Adding More Tables

Real databases often involve many related tables. You can chain JOINs:

```sql
SELECT ...
FROM table1
JOIN table2 ON condition1
JOIN table3 ON condition2
...
```

The order matters logically but the query optimizer may reorder for speed.

slides.title: Example Schema
slides.content:
We'll extend our schema with a `products` table and `order_items`:

```
customers: customer_id, name, city
orders: order_id, customer_id, order_date
order_items: order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity
products: product_id, product_name, price
```

Each order can have multiple items. `order_items` links orders to products.

slides.title: Joining 3 Tables 📎
slides.content:
To get customer names, order IDs, and product names:

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;
```

Notice the chain: customers → orders → order_items → products.

slides.title: Three‑Table JOIN
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY c.name;

quizData.question: When joining multiple tables, what condition do you typically use?

options.text: A condition linking primary key to foreign key between each pair
Any condition involving columns from the tables

quizData.explanation: You join each table to the next using matching key columns, usually PK = FK.

slides.title: Adding Filters and Aggregates ⚙️
slides.content:
You can add WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING after the joins. For example, total revenue per customer from these three tables:

```sql
SELECT c.name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.name;
```

slides.title: Aggregation with Joins
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY total DESC;

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use INNER JOIN by Default, LEFT JOIN When Necessary

With multiple tables, if you use a LEFT JOIN at any step, it will preserve rows from that table even if later joins fail. This can cause unexpected NULLs. Be explicit about your intent.

slides.title: Multi‑Table Practice 🏋️
slides.content: Assume tables: `students(id,name)`, `courses(id,title)`, `enrollments(student_id, course_id, grade)`. Write a query to list each student’s name and the titles of courses they are enrolled in.

slides.title: Multi‑Table Mastery 🎉
slides.content: Now you can traverse an entire database. Let’s combine joins with advanced aggregations.
